documentText.text: Video production, evidence-first
From raw footage to a published, reviewed short.

ShortsOS turns a client's own raw footage into a produced, human-reviewed short — and, when genuinely ready, gets it published with a captured permalink. The steps below are the shape of the pipeline; the publication step is the one we have run for real, end to end.
The pipeline
What actually happens to a client's footage
Existing footage
A client's raw footage — the material already sitting in their own storage — is the starting point. Nothing is generated from a prompt.
Inventory
Footage is technically inspected (duration, resolution, audio presence) and organized into a searchable inventory, so nothing usable gets lost in a folder.
Understanding
Each clip is analyzed for what it actually shows — the moments, not just the file names — to build a record of what evidence exists.
Evidence
Every story candidate is tied back to the specific source moments that support it, with timestamps — so a decision can be checked against the footage, not taken on faith.
Story opportunities
Candidate short-form stories are drafted from that evidence, never invented independently of it.
Human selection
A person decides which opportunity is worth producing. This is a decision checkpoint, not an automatic pipeline.
Production
The selected story is rendered into video, voiced, and captioned.
Review
A human reviews the produced short before anything goes out. Every real run to date has included this checkpoint.
Publication Proven, real run
When a client is genuinely ready, the reviewed short is published — with a captured, checkable permalink.
What's proven
The one thing we can show, not just describe
ShortsOS has completed a real end-to-end Produce → Review → Publish workflow: from source video and render, through human review, to a live Instagram Reel with a captured publication permalink.
For pilots, the workflow is operated by the ShortsOS team.
See the full proof →

documentText.text: Methodology
How the pipeline is built, internally

ShortsOS is operated, not self-directed: an agency team runs the pipeline on a client's behalf. This page describes how that pipeline is architected internally — for transparency about the mechanism, not as a menu of features available to a visitor. Most of what is described here is internal engineering: implemented and tested, but not a capability a customer can invoke directly, and not independently marketed as its own product claim.
Internal architecture
Drive import & inventory
Footage is imported from a client's own storage and organized into a technical inventory (duration, resolution, audio presence).
Media understanding
Clips are analyzed for what they show, building an evidence record used by every later stage.
Opportunity generation
Candidate short-form stories are drafted from that evidence, with the source moments cited alongside each one.
Human decision checkpoint
An operator reviews the candidate opportunities and their supporting evidence before anything is produced.
Production orchestration
The selected opportunity moves through a durable, resumable job pipeline: render, voice, caption.
Render & caption providers
Rendering and captioning are handled by third-party providers behind the pipeline; ShortsOS owns the orchestration and the content decisions, not the underlying video/caption engines.
Review
A human reviews the produced short before publication — a mandatory checkpoint, not an optional one.
Publish & permalink capture
When ready, the reviewed short is published and its permalink is captured and recorded.
What this program actually claims publicly

As of this program's most recent internal review, the underlying capability inventory behind this pipeline is tracked on a four-way scale — proven-and-public, candidate, internal-only, and blocked — and exactly one capability has cleared the bar for a public claim: the end-to-end Produce → Review → Publish workflow described on the Proof page. Everything else described on this page is internal architecture context, not an independent public claim.

documentText.text: Proof
One real, end-to-end run — not a demo

This is the one thing ShortsOS has proven end to end, for real: a single client's raw footage went through production, a human review, and publication — resulting in a live Instagram Reel with a permalink we captured. It is one documented run, not a demonstration reel and not a repeated or automated process.
The claim, exactly as ratified
ShortsOS has completed a real end-to-end Produce → Review → Publish workflow: from source video and render, through human review, to a live Instagram Reel with a captured publication permalink.
For pilots, the workflow is operated by the ShortsOS team.
What happened

Source footage was rendered into a short, reviewed by a person, and published to a real, operator-bound Instagram account. The published post's permalink was captured and stored as the durable record of that publication. Two real adapter defects were found and fixed against the live Instagram integration during this run — evidence that the run was against the real provider, not a mock.
What this is not

This is not a portfolio of many published shorts, not a rendered demo reel, and not a claim about how the finished video looks or performs. It is a record that the mechanism — from source footage to a captured, checkable publication permalink — has actually run once, for real.
Known limits
Single real run is not a load or reliability proof; discovered Instagram adapter defects were fixed reactively against that one live run, not pre-emptively.
Never claimed
The following are explicitly out of bounds for this claim, by ratified governance decision — not just informal caution:
Any claim of automatic publishing without human review — the Review step is a mandatory human checkpoint in every real run to date.
Any claim of guaranteed creative quality.
Any claim of guaranteed performance or virality for any published content.
Any claim of production-scale or repeated-volume proof beyond the one documented real run.
Any claim of universal availability — this workflow is operated by the ShortsOS team for pilots, never generally/instantly available.
Any claim that a customer can connect their own Instagram account to this workflow.
Any claim that a customer can publish directly themselves through this workflow.
Any claim that any end user can self-serve run this loop today — it is operator-run, on one bound Instagram account.
Governance record: docs/governance/publication/2026-09-13-m1-public-marketable-ratification.md (in the ShortsOS product repository).

documentText.text: FAQ
Honest answers, including the ones that are "no"
Can I connect my own Instagram account?
Not yet. The one real publish we have run used a single account operated by the ShortsOS team. There is no independent account connection today.
Can I publish directly myself, without going through ShortsOS?
No. Publishing happens through the ShortsOS team as part of an operated pilot, not as something a customer triggers directly.
Does ShortsOS publish automatically, without anyone reviewing it first?
No. A human reviews every produced short before it is published. That review step has been part of every real run to date, and it is not optional.
Is this available to anyone right now?
No. ShortsOS is currently operated by the team for pilots — it is not a generally or instantly available product.
Has this been done many times, or at scale?
No. What is proven is one documented, real, end-to-end run. We do not claim production-scale or repeated-volume proof beyond that.
Do you guarantee the video will be good, or that it will perform well?
No. We make no guarantee of creative quality, performance, or virality for any published content.
What exactly is proven, then?
That the full Produce → Review → Publish workflow can run for real: source footage in, a real render, a human review, and a live Instagram Reel out, with its permalink captured.
How do I actually start working with ShortsOS?
Request a pilot. The ShortsOS team will follow up directly to scope a real engagement — there is no independent signup.

In ShortsOS, a human review is a mandatory step before publication
ShortsOS's one real end-to-end run went from source video through a mandatory human review to a live Instagram Reel; nothing was published automatically.

When you hand your raw material to a production partner, the moment that matters is the last one: who approves what goes out under your name. With ShortsOS, that approval is a person, not a setting: the review step is a mandatory human checkpoint before anything is published.
In short
Is there a human review before a short is published?

Yes: in every real ShortsOS run to date, a person reviewed the short before it was published, and that review step is mandatory rather than optional. ShortsOS does not publish automatically without that human checkpoint. For pilots, the workflow is operated by the ShortsOS team, so the review happens inside an operated engagement rather than in a tool a customer runs alone.
Where the review sits

ShortsOS has completed a real end-to-end workflow that goes from source video and render, through human review, to a live Instagram Reel with a captured publication permalink. The review comes after production and before publication, and it is a checkpoint a person has to clear, not a default that can be skipped. In that run, publication went through one Instagram account bound to the ShortsOS operator, not through an account a customer linked. For a brand, that means a person looks at the short before your audience does.
What one real run proves, and what it does not

ShortsOS has run this workflow once, end to end, for real, and that single documented run is the whole of its public proof. One run is not a load or reliability proof, and the defects found in the Instagram connection during it were fixed reactively, against that live run, not beforehand. The review is a checkpoint on what gets published, not a promise of creative quality, performance or virality. When you compare vendors, ask each one to show you its review step in a real run, not only in a diagram.

ShortsOS does not offer this workflow as a generally or instantly available product. A pilot does not include linking your own Instagram account, and it does not let a customer publish directly. documentText.text: Insights · Engineering note · 2026-09-24 · 3 min read
How ShortsOS repaired evidence records that pointed at vanished commits
ShortsOS repaired six evidence records that cited commits no longer in its code history, and left every public claim and status exactly as it was.
Historical record, not an availability claim. This note describes engineering work, cited below by commit. What may be claimed about each capability it mentions is listed at the end of the page.

What a vendor says in public is only as trustworthy as the record that lets someone check it. When that record points at something nobody can retrieve anymore, the claim still reads the same, yet no fresh check can confirm it. In mid-September 2026, ShortsOS found that gap in its own claim records and reproduced it on an untouched copy of its main code line.
In short
What broke, and what was repaired?

Six of the records ShortsOS uses to verify its capability claims cited commits that no longer existed anywhere in its code history, not even as leftovers. A fresh copy of the code, which ShortsOS treats as the authority for verification, cannot fetch a commit that nothing points to, so those records could not be checked there. The repair pointed three of the records at the register entry that documents them, and let the other three check files that still exist in the current code. No public claim, prohibited claim or publication status changed; only the citations used to check them did.
Why a quiet failure mattered

Three days before the repair, on 13 September 2026, the ShortsOS owner ratified one capability, its real produce, review and publish workflow, for a public claim. One of the six broken records belonged to that very capability. On a fresh copy of the code, that broken record silently pushed the capability back to candidate status. A candidate, in this governance vocabulary, is real work that has not been cleared for a public claim. The team logged the problem as a live regression of a ratified decision, not as a cosmetic data issue. A check that breaks loudly tends to get fixed quickly; one that quietly lowers a claim can sit unnoticed.
How the repair was scoped

Three of the records described research documents that were never merged into the main code line and carried no public claim. ShortsOS pointed those three at the register entry that names each document and its gap. The other three cited files that are real and current, so ShortsOS dropped the dead commit reference and let the check read those files as they stand today. Every claim wording and every publication status stayed the same, which kept the repair narrow: it fixed how claims are checked, not what they say. While verifying the repair, the team also found a second, unrelated defect on the untouched main code line. Two governance test fixtures had been written to break on the day a permission they check changed; they broke as designed, and were updated to match.
What it means if you rely on the claim

When you evaluate a vendor, the useful question is whether its proof can be re-checked by someone who was not in the room when it was produced. ShortsOS reproduced this failure on an unmodified copy of its main code line before changing anything, rather than guessing at what had gone wrong. Each repaired record now points at something that exists in the current code or in the register, where a fresh copy can find it.

Why ShortsOS chose to make one public claim, not nine
ShortsOS classified 39 capabilities, found nine candidates and ratified exactly one for a public claim, with eight guardrails on how it may be described.
Historical record, not an availability claim. This note describes engineering work, cited below by commit. What may be claimed about each capability it mentions is listed at the end of the page.

It is tempting for a young product to present all it has built as something you can buy. The question a buyer needs answered is narrower: which of those things has been shown to work for real, and on what terms? In September 2026, ShortsOS answered that question for itself and ratified a single capability for a public claim.
In short
Why only one public claim?

When ShortsOS first classified its 39 finished capabilities against its own evidence, none of them qualified for a public claim, nine became candidates, 30 stayed internal and three concepts were blocked outright. The rule was then amended so that a capability the ShortsOS team operates for its clients could qualify, on the condition that it is not described as something customers run on their own. Of the nine candidates, exactly one already met that bar in its own wording, and the owner ratified it on 13 September 2026.
Four facts kept apart for each capability

ShortsOS keeps four facts about each capability apart on purpose: whether it is built, how strongly a real run proves it, who can reach it today, and what may be said about it in public. The last of those four is never set by hand; it is derived, and any single failing condition keeps a capability below a public claim instead of being averaged away. Three concepts sit in a blocked column that no amount of evidence can lift: customers publishing to Instagram without the team, customers linking their own Google Drive, and general promises about creative quality.
The rule change, and the one promotion

On 13 September 2026, ShortsOS amended that rule so a capability operated by the team for pilots could reach a public claim, matching the way the product was ratified to be sold: through a pilot request rather than a sign-up. The change came with conditions: such a capability qualifies only if its own wording avoids any customer-run framing and its list of prohibited claims already rules that framing out. Re-run against the nine candidates, the amended rule let exactly one through on its existing wording: the real produce, review and publish workflow. Two other capabilities were one wording edit away from qualifying, and the owner chose not to promote them, because they document individual suppliers behind the workflow rather than something a customer needs to hear about.
What was refused, in writing

The owner rejected an earlier draft saying the team “runs your full pipeline for you”, judging it stronger than one real run can support. The ratified capability carries eight prohibited claims, among them any suggestion that a customer runs it alone, publishes directly, or receives guaranteed quality, performance or virality. Alongside the classification, ShortsOS added a rule that asks, whenever governed product code changes, whether the change has a public-content consequence and whether anyone said so on purpose. A governed change that arrives without such a record is treated as a hard failure, not as a warning. For a buyer, the useful sign is not how many claims a vendor makes, but whether each one can be traced to the evidence behind it.

Why ShortsOS made zero a valid answer when searching footage for stories
In September 2026, ShortsOS let its story search report no strong story, stopped reading file dates as filming dates and fixed a cross-client lookup.
Historical record, not an availability claim. This note describes engineering work, cited below by commit. What may be claimed about each capability it mentions is listed at the end of the page.

Anyone who has handed a pile of raw clips to a tool knows the risk: the tool finds something, whether or not it is really there. ShortsOS changed its own story search so that finding no strong story became an honest result rather than an error. Its register lists this work as internal engineering with no independent public claim, so read it as history, not as a feature list.
In short
What changed, in short?

The story search in ShortsOS was moved from expecting three to seven strong stories to a rule of zero to three, where zero is a distinct, honest outcome. Technical failures, unfinished analysis and runs paused for budget stay separate outcomes, so a failure is not reported as a weak story. Two related fixes followed the same logic: filming dates are no longer guessed from file dates, and duplicate checks no longer look across clients.
Why no story can be the right answer

Before the change, a search that found only one or two stories backed by the footage was rejected, and a search that found none was filed under the same rejection. After it, one, two or three stories backed by evidence are accepted, capped at three only once the evidence check has run, and zero gets its own outcome: no strong story available. The same change keeps technical trouble apart from editorial judgement, so a failed or paused run is not presented as footage without a story. For a brand, that distinction decides whether a no is information about its footage or noise from a system.
Dates and duplicates, fixed for the same reason

ShortsOS used to record a clip's filming time straight from the date the file was last modified in Google Drive, a date that changes whenever a file is copied, re-shared or re-uploaded. The fix reads the time embedded in the video first, then explicit metadata, then what the client declared, and otherwise marks the date as unknown, recording disagreements instead of averaging them. Where no reliable date exists, the product is built to show unknown rather than invent one. A separate check that spots duplicate clips compared files across all clients with no filter, so one client's clip could be reported as a duplicate of another client's. The corrected check only looks within the client that owns the clip. That fix was proven against an isolated test database with four regression cases, which is not proof of isolation under real load across many clients.
Similar takes are grouped, not thrown away

When a shoot produces several takes of the same moment, ShortsOS groups them rather than excluding any clip merely because it looks similar to another. All clips still appear in the results, and supporting evidence is counted by distinct group, so three takes of one moment do not pass for three separate proofs. The grouping relies on signals the system already recorded, uses no AI similarity model, and does not judge what two clips mean. Taken together, these fixes make the pipeline readier to say what it does not know.

documentText.text: Request a pilot
Thanks for reaching out

This page confirms what happens next — it is not a submission receipt. This site has no server or database behind it, so it has no way to confirm an email actually reached us; that confirmation lives in your own email client's sent folder, not here.
What happens next
If you emailed us from the Request a pilot page, someone from the ShortsOS team will reply directly to that email, usually within a few business days.

If you don't hear back, check your sent folder to confirm the email actually went out, and feel free to send it again — there is no automated queue or ticketing system on our side that could silently drop it, but there is also no automated acknowledgment.
